think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 32-year-old male presents with a painless erythematous plaque on the neck and chest that has indolently persisted for 9 years and ulcerated with draining sinus tracts over the past 2 years, associated with significant systemic weight loss (15 kg). Despite the protracted course and prior failure of systemic antibiotics and topical antiseptics, he lacks classical pulmonary complaints such as cough, fever, or night sweats. The clinical presentation challenges the clinician to distinguish between chronic refractory pyogenic bacterial infection, deep fungal granuloma, cutaneous malignancy/lymphoma, systemic vasculitis, and contiguous mycobacterial lymphadenitis.

2. Admission Breakpoint: Evaluation concludes at the completion of initial clinical history, physical examination of the cutaneous lesions and lymph nodes, baseline triage blood work (CBC showing moderate anemia, markedly elevated ESR and hs-CRP, inverted albumin/globulin ratio), and baseline sonography/radiology (ultrasound demonstrating cervical/axillary lymphadenopathy with liquefactive changes and splenomegaly; chest CT demonstrating bilateral fibrous scars and minor basilar inflammation), strictly before receiving targeted mycobacterial immunodiagnostics (PPD, interferon-gamma release assays), sputum mycobacterial cultures, and invasive histopathologic biopsy.

3. Differential Distinctions: Chronic bacterial cellulitis/abscess is ruled out by refractoriness to conventional antibiotics and non-suppurative histopathology. Deep fungal infections (e.g., actinomycosis, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis) are excluded by negative fungal staining. Vasculitis and lymphoma/malignancy are ruled out by unremarkable autoimmune/tumor markers and lymph node histopathology demonstrating caseating granulomatous inflammation.
case_prompt:
A 32-year-old male presented to the outpatient medical center complaining of an extensive, painless erythematous plaque involving his anterior neck and chest region that had been present for 9 years and had ulcerated 2 years prior to presentation. The lesions had initially appeared 9 years ago as small, asymptomatic papules and nodules on his neck for which he did not seek treatment. Over time, the lesions expanded into confluent plaques and nodules across the neck and chest and developed ulcerations with discharging tracts. He had previously been diagnosed with a cutaneous bacterial infection and completed empirical courses of systemic oral antibiotics and topical iodine without improvement. Over the preceding year, the patient experienced an unintentional 15-kg weight loss; however, he denied fevers, chills, productive cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, or arthralgias. Past medical history was notable for a treated chronic pulmonary infection 12 years prior, for which he had completed a 6-month multidrug antimicrobial regimen.

Physical examination revealed a 3 cm × 5 cm erythematous plaque with ulceration and friable granulation tissue on the chest wall. Surrounding the plaque were multiple 1 cm × 2 cm erythematous nodules and plaques draining via visible sinus tracts over the neck and chest. Palpation of the peripheral lymph node basins demonstrated multiple enlarged, mobile bilateral cervical and axillary lymph nodes measuring approximately 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm. The remainder of the systemic examination was normal.

Baseline laboratory investigations revealed a hemoglobin level of 85 g/L (reference 130–175 g/L) indicating moderate normocytic anemia. Inflammatory markers were markedly elevated, with a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein of 63.7 mg/L (reference < 5 mg/L) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 120 mm/h (reference < 15 mm/h). Serum biochemistry revealed an albumin of 30.6 g/L and an elevated globulin of 43.5 g/L. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA) and serum tumor markers were within normal reference ranges.

Superficial lymph node ultrasonography identified multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral neck and axillary regions with features of partial liquefactive abscess formation. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated moderate splenomegaly. Chest computed tomography (CT) demonstrated bilateral fibrous pulmonary foci and minor inflammatory changes in the lower lobe of the left lung, along with multiple mildly enlarged bilateral axillary lymph nodes.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Pyogenic Bacterial Skin Infection / Chronic Abscess
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The patient was initially diagnosed with and treated for a routine bacterial cutaneous infection with systematic antibiotics and topical iodine, but failed to show any improvement and lesions steadily progressed over several years.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He was diagnosed with cutaneous infection and treated with systematic antibiotics and topical iodine, but the lesions did not improve and gradually worsened.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Active pulmonary involvement was considered given his history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis 12 years prior and bilateral fibrous foci on CT, but was excluded by the lack of pulmonary symptoms, stable fibrous lung changes, and negative sputum examinations.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: CT scan result and multiple sputum cultures excluded the possibility of pulmonary tuberculosis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Ulcerative chronic nodules and fistulae can indicate endemic or opportunistic fungal infections, but periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) fungal stains of the biopsied tissue were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: PAS stain and acid-fast stain from skin specimen were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic turning point was established by excisional biopsy of a cervical lymph node revealing classic caseating granulomatous inflammation, corroborated by highly elevated T-SPOT interferon-gamma release assay (1904.18 pg/mL) and a positive tuberculin skin test (15 mm induration), confirming scrofuloderma with subsequent complete resolution following four-drug anti-tuberculosis therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A biopsy of left cervical lymph node showed granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis.

editor_comments: Successfully distilled into Stanford MedCaseReasoning format. Admission prompt strictly removes all mycobacterial pathogen identifiers, past specific TB diagnostic labels, and invasive biopsy/T-spot results while preserving clinical timeline, vitals, exam, baseline labs, and imaging. Diagnostic reasoning highlights differentials and provides verbatim supporting quotes.
